ana.nudge.sig-heart: Look at the bar of power: which part draws the most, and what decides how much it has to send?
ana.nudge.sig-bearing: Watch the line of tones while you move the sampling rate. Where is the edge, and on which side of it is the warning tone?
ana.nudge.reg-jobs: Try all three on each job. One may fail for a reason you can read. Of those that work, compare what reaches the chip and how many parts it takes.
ana.note: A teaching model with round numbers, not any product. Real chains also filter before sampling, compress what they send and sleep between measurements.
ana.tone.lost: The warning tone lies past half the sampling rate and is folded back.
ana.tone.kept: The warning tone lies below half the sampling rate.
ana.tone.far: half the rate is off this line
ana.tone.ghost: Tones from slow (left) to fast (right). Past half the sampling rate nothing can be told apart: the warning tone shows up as a tone at {v} Hz that is not there.
ana.tone.ok: Tones from slow (left) to fast (right): the motor's hum, and further right the warning tone. It lies below half the sampling rate, so it is seen where it is.
ana.reg.aria: Battery, regulator and chip: {e}% of the energy reaches the chip, {h} becomes heat.
ana.reg.ldo.d: burns the difference as heat; parts: {n}
ana.reg.buck.d: chops, then smooths with a coil; parts: {n}
ana.reg.both.d: the big step, then a clean-up; parts: {n}
ana.job.wearable.why: A fitness band, asleep 95% of the time.
ana.job.cpu.why: A phone processor running flat out.
ana.job.nearly.why: A radio fed from a supply only a little higher than it needs.
ana.reg.draw2: It draws {a} for {pa}% of the time and {b} in short bursts.
ana.reg.tol: Its supply may wobble by {v} at most.
ana.reg.cool: The regulator may give off {v} of heat at most.
ana.reg.flow: Of every 100 units of energy from the battery, {e} reach the chip and {h} become heat.
ana.reg.start: Pick a regulator to put between the battery and the chip.
ana.rh.dropout: The input must be higher than the output by at least the regulator's dropout.
ana.rh.ripple: Too much ripple: the switching leaves more on the output than this load can tolerate.
ana.rh.heat: Too hot: a lot of heat in one small part. The extra voltage has to go somewhere.
ana.rh.best-ldo: The best choice here. The input is barely above the output, so a linear regulator wastes almost nothing and needs no coil.
ana.rh.best-buck: The best choice here. Switching wastes far less power than burning the voltage difference as heat.
ana.rh.best-both: The best choice here. The buck does the big step efficiently; the small LDO after it removes the ripple.
ana.rh.works: It works, but another choice is better here. Compare efficiency, heat, ripple and the number of parts.
ana.rh.first: It works. Is it the best here? Try another and compare.
ana.reg.note: A teaching model with round values. Real regulators vary widely, and many switch to a low-power mode at light loads.
srv.q.intro: Quantization rounds each weight to the nearest value a short number format can hold, after dividing by a scale so that the biggest still fits. An outlier is a rare weight far bigger than the rest. 20 dB means the weights stand ten times above the rounding error.
srv.q.aria: The weights as trained, a bell curve, and as stored at {bits} bits each: steps. {zero} of the weights are stored as zero.
srv.q.x: a weight's value (1 = an ordinary weight)
srv.q.legend: Grey: the weights as trained. Line: as stored; every weight in a step becomes the one value marked below it. Red: the weights that become zero.
srv.q.legendBlock: Grey: the weights as trained. Line: as stored in a typical block; every weight in a step becomes the one value marked below it. Red: the weights that become zero.
srv.q.legendFine: The steps are too fine to see: stored and trained weights lie on one line.
srv.q.mapAria: Every setting tried: the memory its weights take, against how far the signal stands above the rounding error.
srv.q.mapLegend: Each dot is a setting you have tried; the large one is where you are. The green corner is the goal.
srv.q.verdict.lossless: Practically lossless: the rounding error is far below the noise in training.
srv.q.verdict.small: Small error. With careful calibration, models usually keep their accuracy.
srv.q.verdict.noticeable: Noticeable error. Models need fine-tuning or finer-grained scaling to cope.
srv.q.zeros: {v} of the weights collapsed to zero, because the biggest weight sharing their scale stretched it.
srv.q.is16: A 16-bit format reaches far enough by itself, so it takes no scale.
srv.q.hint: One big weight sets the scale for every weight that shares it. What if fewer weights shared each scale? And what do the scales themselves cost?
srv.q.done: Only FP4 with one scale for every block of 16 weights works: 39.4 GB and about 20.5 dB. One scale for all the weights lets a few large outliers crush every small weight to zero. Small blocks keep each scale local, at the cost of half a bit a weight.
srv.q.note: A teaching model: {n} sample weights from a bell curve, rounded by each format's own rules. The layers of a real model differ from each other.
srv.e.aria: The energy of one token: {a} reaches the AI chip, {s} goes to the rest of the server and its network, {c} to cooling and power losses.
srv.e.legend: A band's thickness is its energy. The bar at the left is what comes in from the grid; its dashed outline is where it started.
srv.e.set.pue: PUE: watts the building draws for each watt its computers use
srv.e.set.overhead: Rest of the server and its network, on top of the chip
srv.e.say.same: An answer costs what it did at the start.
srv.e.say.less: An answer now costs {v}% less than at the start.
srv.e.say.more: An answer now costs {v}% more than at the start.
srv.e.say.building: The best building you found saved {v}%.
srv.e.hint: Look at which band is thickest. The building can only trim its own bands. An answer's energy is power divided by tokens a second: which of the two can move furthest?
srv.e.done: Even a near-perfect building saves less than a third, because most of the energy was reaching the chip all along. The rest has to come from the chip itself: more tokens out of the same watts. That is why services answer many people at once, and why AI chips are judged by tokens per joule.
srv.e.note: A simple model: the chip's power, plus the rest of the server as a share of it, times the building's PUE (the extra goes to cooling and to losses in the power supply), divided by tokens a second. Here every dial moves freely; in a real hall they are tied to each other.
srv.p.intro: Reading (prefill) keeps the chip's arithmetic busy with every token at once. Writing (decode) waits, for each token, while memory hands over every weight.
srv.p.aria: One request in time: reading the prompt takes {read}, then writing the answer takes {write}.
srv.p.legend: Block: the whole prompt, read at once. Stripes: the answer, token after token (one stripe: {k}).
srv.p.say.prefill: Reading takes longer: the chip's arithmetic is the limit.
srv.p.say.decode: Writing takes longer: memory is the limit.
srv.p.say.times: Token for token, reading is {v} times faster than writing.
srv.p.say.chips: The model is too big for one chip's memory, so it is spread over {n}.
srv.p.hint: Compare how fast one token is read with how fast one is written. How many times longer than the answer must the prompt be to even that out?
srv.p.done: It takes a prompt of about 77,000 tokens. Reading works on all the prompt's tokens at once, so the chip computes at full speed; writing produces one token at a time and waits for memory each time. Token for token, reading is about 280 times faster.
srv.p.note: A simple model: reading uses half of the chip's top arithmetic speed; each written token takes as long as reading every weight from memory. The chips' speeds and memories are their makers' own figures.
rd.aria: The chip's blocks drawn as their copies and voters; the whole chip is right {v} of the time.
rd.legend: Each tile is one copy of a block, as wide as the block is big; the wedge is the voter, which passes on what most copies say. On the right, how often each block still gives a wrong answer.
rd.r.none: Run a thousand chips to watch the copies fail and the votes hold.
rd.intro: Every block of this chip sometimes gives a wrong answer, the big ones most often, and the chip is right only when every block is. A block can be built three or five times, with a voter that takes the majority. Each copy takes floor, and the voter can be wrong too.
rd.msg.met: The whole chip is now right more often than its worst part alone. Copies of the flaky blocks outvote their bad moments; the small, steady blocks were left alone.
rd.msg.worse: Voting made the {b} worse: it rarely goes wrong on its own, and the voter adds a chance of its own to go wrong.
rd.msg.big: Too much floor: the copies no longer fit the chip. Which blocks gain least from their copies?
rd.msg.close: The whole is already more reliable than its worst part. Not yet enough: where would one more copy help most?
rd.msg.bare: Built once each, the whole chip goes wrong far more often than any one part: every flaw adds up.
rd.msg.more: Better. The blocks that fail most still pull the whole chip down.
rd.hint: A vote only pays where a block goes wrong much more often than the voter. Start with the blocks that fail most, compare what three and five copies buy for their floor, and leave the steady small blocks as they are.
rd.done: A whole more reliable than its parts, for a price in floor, power and speed. With smaller switches every part grows flakier, and the question comes back harder: where does voting stop paying, and what else can a whole do?
rd.note: A teaching model with round numbers: each copy goes wrong at random, independently of the others, and the voter is one part with its own small chance of being wrong. Left out: faults that hit every copy at once (a shared supply, a shared clock, the same design mistake), the time the vote takes, and codes that fix errors with fewer copies.
mo.aria: A network on a chip, its first chip right {own}% of the time and its copies {copied}%.
mo.fig.first.sw: the first chip, written from software
mo.legend: A grid is a layer kept as bits; a wave, a layer kept as analog cells. Each copy is coloured by how often it answers right: green at 90% or better, amber above 85%, red below. The line on the energy bars is the goal.
mo.t.energy: goal: at most {v}% of all bits
mo.intro: A small network reads a sensor and answers. Kept as bits, its numbers copy exactly, but every answer moves them, and moving bits costs energy. Kept as the state of analog cells, it computes for far less, but no two cells, and no two chips, are quite alike.
mo.learn.software: In software, then written to the chip
mo.cal: Each copy relearns a little on its own chip
mo.msg.met: Cheap, right on its own chip, and copyable, at the price of a few minutes of relearning on every copy. A brain pays the other price: it never copies at all.
mo.msg.digital: All bits: exact, copyable, and every answer pays to move every number.
mo.msg.costly: Still costly: most of each answer's energy goes on the layers kept as bits.
mo.msg.brain: Like a brain: it learned around its own chip's quirks and works well there, but on any other chip those quirks are wrong. What it knows dies with the chip.
mo.msg.blind: Learned in software, it copies faithfully, but it never saw this chip's quirks, so every chip, the first too, answers worse.
mo.msg.more: Close. One of the three still falls short.
mo.hint: Try the three ways of learning at a high analog share, and watch the copies change colour. Learning on the chip fits one chip; learning in software fits none exactly. What if each copy fits itself?
mo.done: Copyable and cheap, but only by relearning on every copy, and the more is analog, the longer that takes. Is that a machine that copies its mind, or one that grows a new one each time from a shared start?
mo.note: A teaching model with round numbers, not measurements: analog layers about twelve times cheaper per answer than bits, every analog cell off by about 10%, and accuracy falling with the square of the noise. Left out: cells that drift with time and heat, the cost of the converters at each layer's edge, and networks trained to tolerate noise.
xray.type.dram.clue: Huge, extremely dense arrays split by thin strips: almost the whole die is memory.
xray.type.pixels.clue: A vast field of tiny coloured squares: one light-sensitive pixel each, under red, green and blue filters.
xray.type.adc.clue: A long, thin strip of identical columns along the pixel array: one converter for each column of pixels.
xr.why.mcu: Most of the area is memory (flash for the program, SRAM to work in) and analog circuits that talk to the outside world. The processor itself is a speck.
xr.why.phone: A block for each job: big and little processor cores, graphics, an AI engine, image and video engines, and memory links along the edge.
xr.why.gpu: A sea of identical cores, with a band of cache across the middle and links to the stacked memory down both sides.
xr.why.dram: Almost the whole die is memory arrays, with a thin strip of control logic and a row of pads down the middle.
xr.why.camera: Most of the area is the pixel array, with a row of converters above and below it, one for each column of pixels.
xr.ask: What kind of chip is this?
xr.wiring: That is wiring and spacing between the blocks.
xr.g.found: Every block found on one die
xr.cleared: Dies read to the last block: {n}
xr.aria: A photo of a chip's die, its blocks drawn with the textures they have under a microscope.
xr.done: You can read a die: memory as a regular grid, logic as fine noise, copies of one tile, hand-drawn shapes, and the share of area that tells what a chip is for. A die photo is one way to check a chip; what is hidden below the top layer, or in its design, is the harder part.
er.intro: From the job the chip does down to its package, each row is a level of the chip: the wrong values born there, what that level's protection stops, and the protection itself. What gets past every level leaves at the top as silent wrong answers, counted in every billion answers.
er.placed.phone: A 2-second answer from an assistant on the phone, with 64 megabits of memory in use.
er.placed.car: One millisecond step of a brake controller, through fifteen hot years. The car standard at its highest level asks for fewer than 10 failures in a billion hours.
er.placed.datacentre: A large language model writing an answer in a hall of machines, where rare for one machine is daily for the hall.
er.placed.space: One second of a satellite's computer, built like a car's, in low orbit, where particles flip bits thousands of times more often.
er.inHours: in a billion hours of work
er.bornT: {v} wrong values born here in a billion answers
er.stopT: {v} stopped here in a billion answers
er.nohall: Only a hall of machines can take some out to test them.
er.msg.met: Right enough, within what this place allows. About {caught} answers in a billion are still caught: refused or redone, never wrong.
er.msg.costly: Being right costs more area or energy than this place allows. Which protection buys least here?
er.msg.worst: Most of the silent answers left come from {src}. Which level can see them?
er.all: Phone, car and data centre cleared: the same faults, met at different levels by each.
er.hint: Look at where the silent answers are born, and protect at a level that can see them: codes on memory for flipped bits, a margin for late signals, copies or self-test for copies born broken. A car must pay for a second copy of its logic; a data centre cannot, but it can check its arithmetic and hunt bad machines in the fleet.
er.done: Silent errors can be made rare, never impossible, and each power of ten costs more. When no one can check every answer, what is the trust in a machine resting on?
er.note: The puzzle's engine (src/engines/errors.js): the rates of particles, broken copies and stopping machines are from sources, the rest are choices said to be in the code. It is fair enough to compare plans and never wrong in direction, not a reliability simulator.
carch.intro: A core is a set of choices. Three are real ones in RISC-V cores: a multiplier or none, one arithmetic unit or two, 32 registers or 16. Each change runs the puzzles' programs again and says what it buys (cycles) and what it costs: area on the chip, counted in transistors, and energy.
carch.aria: Your core as a floor plan, every part's area to scale beside the plain core and the area allowed, and its program running cycle by cycle.
carch.fig.cap: Left, the core drawn to scale: each part's area is its share of the transistors, lit while the program uses it. Right, the program's run: each row is a cycle; with two units, two instructions that do not depend on each other go in the same cycle.
carch.mul.none.d: Multiplying is a loop of additions and shifts, as in the Multiply puzzle.
carch.mul.slow.d: One adder used 32 times over, one bit of the number a cycle: small, and always 32 cycles.
carch.mul.fast.d: An array of adders that works out every bit at once: one cycle, and about as big as the rest of the core together.
carch.alus.2.d: Two instructions in one cycle when the second does not need the first one's answer, and they do not both use memory. The registers need more ways in and out.
carch.regs.16.d: RV32E, RISC-V's base for small embedded cores: half the register file. These programs only use the first 16, so they still run.
carch.v.won: Twice as fast in the area allowed, for less energy. Every part of it earns its place: the multiplier turns a long loop into one instruction, the second unit pairs what does not depend on each other, and half the registers make the room.
carch.v.plain: The plain core: one unit, no multiplier, 32 registers. Every other core is measured against it.
carch.v.both: {s} faster, but not fast enough, and already {a} the area.
carch.v.big: Fast enough at {s}, but {a} the area: too big. What could make room?
carch.v.bigslow: {a} the area, over what is allowed, and only {s} faster.
carch.v.slow: {s} faster in {a} the area: not fast enough yet.
carch.v.energy: Fast enough and small enough, but it uses {e} the plain core's energy.
carch.watch: Watch a program run on it
carch.bars.aria: Each program's cycles on the plain core and on yours.
carch.hint: No single change gets there. Look at what each one costs on the floor plan: the fast multiplier alone doubles the core. The slow one and a second unit together are fast enough but too big, so ask what the programs do not use.
carch.done: This is how cores are chosen: not the biggest, but the one that fits the work. A phone, a car and a data centre want different answers to the same three questions.
carch.note: A sketch, said plainly: the programs are the puzzles' own, run on the lab's simulator and timed again for your core; one cycle an instruction, a slow multiply 32; area counted in transistors (a slice of the arithmetic unit is 148, a register bit 24); energy is what each instruction switches plus what the whole core leaks every cycle it is on. Figures are compared to the plain core, never quoted as watts.
rv.intro: The core of the community's computer runs RISC-V. Each puzzle puts its numbers in a1 and a2; your program leaves the answer in a0. Run checks it on every case twice: on the lab's reference core, and on a core whose arithmetic unit is your own ALU slice, copied 32 times. Play sends each instruction through that core's datapath, the wires and units it uses.
rv.aria: Your core's datapath: the program, the decoder showing {op}, the registers, the arithmetic unit made of 32 slices, the memory, and the wire that writes the answer back.
rv.err.label: there is no label called {n}.
rv.err.unknown: {n} is not an instruction this core knows.
rv.err.range: {n} is too big for this instruction.
rv.err.operands: this instruction needs a different number of operands.
rv.err.memop: write a memory address as offset(register), for example 0(t0).
rv.err.mem: the program reached outside the memory.
rv.err.needM: {n} needs a multiplier, and this core has none.
rv.err.needMAC: {n} needs the AI unit, and this core has none.
rv.err.needDOT4: {n} needs the AI unit's four-way multiplier, which this core does not have.
rv.forbid: This puzzle is to be solved without {op}.
rv.slow: Right, but it takes {v} cycles. There is a way with far fewer.
rv.p.sum.d: a0 = 1 + 2 + … + a1. This one already works: run it and watch the loop go round.
rv.p.max.d: a0 = the larger of a1 and a2. A branch skips a line when a comparison is true.
rv.p.mul.d: a0 = a1 × a2. This core has no multiplier: build one from additions.
rv.p.fib.d: a0 = the a1-th number of 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 …, each the sum of the two before it.
rv.p.fast.d: a0 = 1 + 2 + … + a1 again, now with a multiplier, in 12 cycles or fewer even for a1 = 1000.
rv.ok.sum: Solved. Every turn of the loop is three instructions; adding to 100 takes about 300 steps.
rv.ok.max: Solved. A compare and a jump: that is all an "if" is, inside a processor.
rv.ok.mul: Solved, with additions only. Early processors multiplied this way; a multiplier in hardware does it in one step, for the price of its area.
rv.ok.fib: Solved. Two registers carry the last two numbers, and a third makes the next.
rv.ok.fast: Solved: the same answer in a handful of cycles, by an idea instead of a loop. Better hardware or a better idea: which do you reach for first?
rv.hint.sum: Press Run, then Play. Watch t2 count up and a0 grow, and the branch jump back to the top of the loop.
rv.hint.max: Copy a1 into a0 with mv. Then compare: if a1 is already at least a2 (bge), jump past the line that copies a2 into a0.
rv.hint.mul: Add a1 to a0 again and again, taking 1 from a2 each time (addi a2, a2, -1), until a2 is zero (beq a2, x0, done).
rv.hint.fib: Keep the last two numbers in a0 and t1 (start with 0 and 1). Each turn: t2 = a0 + t1, then a0 = t1, then t1 = t2, and take 1 from a1.
rv.hint.fast: 1 + 2 + … + n is n × (n + 1) ÷ 2. Add 1 to a1, multiply (mul), then halve with a shift to the right (srli).
rv.done: Three programs on an open processor. Every app, game and AI model is made of steps like these, only billions of them a second, on cores like this one copied many times.
rv.note: The lab's RISC-V simulator (RV32I, the integer instructions, and the M extension for the last puzzle), from the first site's RISC-V lab; your core runs the same instructions with every add, subtract, compare and logic step done by your slice. One instruction takes one cycle here; a real core overlaps several at once.
srch.intro: One circuit, made two ways. A person designed it with care: that is the flat line. A blind search changes a circuit at random, checks it on the inputs, and keeps the change if it is no worse. Give the search more circuits to try, and watch where it passes the person.
srch.aria: Smallest working circuit found: {best} cells. The person's design: {hand} cells.
srch.legend: The line steps down each time the search finds a smaller circuit that passes the checker. A cell is one gate of the studio's library. The squares are the eight input patterns, for the best circuit within the budget: ✓ right, ✗ wrong.
srch.g.beat: Search beats the person, every input checked
srch.g.fooled: Checker tries half: search "wins", and is wrong
srch.msg.none: Within {b} circuits tried, nothing is right on every input checked yet. Spend more.
srch.msg.beat: Within {b} circuits tried, the search found a circuit of {c} cells, right on every input: smaller than the person's {h}.
srch.msg.tie: Within {b} circuits tried, the search matches the person: {c} cells. Spend more to see if it passes.
srch.msg.bigger: Within {b} circuits tried, the search's best is right but bigger than the person's: {c} cells against {h}. Spend more.
srch.msg.fooled: The checker passed a circuit of {c} cells, far smaller than the person's {h}. On all {n} inputs it is right on only {r}: it learned the test, not the job.
srch.msg.wrong: The checker passed a circuit of {c} cells that is right on only {r} of the {n} inputs, though not yet smaller than the person's {h}.
srch.msg.lucky: The checker passed a circuit of {c} cells, and by luck it is right on every input, even those never tried.
srch.hint.beat: Keep the voter and every input, and raise the computing until the line drops under the person's. A wider circuit needs far more.
srch.hint.fooled: Now let the checker try only half the inputs, and look at the squares under the curve.
srch.done: Both seen. More computing wins where every answer can be checked; where the checker sees only part, the search wins the test and fails the job. What can be checked, and by whom?
srch.note: From Rich Sutton's essay The Bitter Lesson (2019, incompleteideas.net). The search is the lab's evolve engine (Cartesian genetic programming, Miller and Thomson, 2000): each round it tries four changed copies of the best circuit. Size is counted in cells after the studio's synthesis, for the person's design and the search's alike. One run is one seed: another run may cross earlier or later.
halt.intro1: A gate is a tiny decision: two inputs in, one output out. Pick a material, then make the output go off only when both A and B are on. Tap A and B to try them.
halt.intro2: An agent claims it can tell whether any program stops. Its method: run the program for a budget of steps. If it has stopped, it says "stops"; if not, it guesses "never stops". Build programs from blocks, run them on the community's RISC-V core, and prove it wrong.
halt.g.aria: A gate made of {m}: A is {a}, B is {b}, the output is {o}.
halt.out.water.follow: the cup fills from the pipe
halt.out.domino.follow: the row topples the last domino
halt.out.domino.invert: the row breaks a second row
halt.cap.water.follow: A tank on the left. Water reaches the cup only through open valves.
halt.cap.water.invert: A second tank keeps the cup full; water that gets through the valves drains it away.
halt.cap.light.follow: A lamp on the left. Its light reaches the output only through open shutters.
halt.cap.light.invert: A second lamp lights the output; light that gets through the shutters closes a shade in front of it.
halt.cap.domino.follow: A push on the left. The row topples through a gap only where a domino stands in it.
halt.cap.domino.invert: A second row topples down to the output; a row that gets through the gaps knocks a domino out of it first, and the output stays standing.
halt.msg.and: Yours is on only when both are on: an AND gate. Close, but the wanted output is the other way round.
halt.msg.or: Yours is on when either is on: an OR gate. Not yet.
halt.msg.nor: Yours is off when either is on: a NOR gate. Almost: the wanted one is off only when both are on.
halt.msg.nand: That is a NAND gate: off only when both are on. From this one kind of gate every other can be built, in any material.
halt.l.aria: Two gates, each feeding the other. The bit holds {q}.
halt.l.notfed: not fed back: each gate only answers its own push
halt.l.cap: Two of your gates. Push Set or Reset: without feedback, the bit falls back as soon as you let go.
halt.l.capFed: Each gate's output now feeds the other's input, so each holds the other where it is after the push is gone.
halt.ui.fed: Feed each output back into the other gate
halt.push.set.0: While you pushed, the bit showed 1. You let go, and it fell back to 0: it forgot.
halt.push.reset.0: The bit shows 0. Without feedback it is always back to 0 once you let go, so it remembers nothing.
halt.push.set.1f: Pushed and let go: the bit still shows 1. The two gates hold each other: it remembers.
halt.push.reset.0f: Reset and let go: the bit shows 0 and stays 0. A bit that holds either way is memory.
halt.pattern: A processor is a very large number of such gates in a pattern. Silicon is only the material that makes them small, fast and cheap: a computer is a pattern, not a material.
halt.ui.deeper: Go deeper: the program nobody can judge
halt.hint.gate: The output should be off in one row only: when both are on. Try one after the other, with an output that is on unless something gets through.
halt.hint.bit: Feed each output back, then push Set, then push Reset.
halt.note1: Teaching models of the pattern, not working machines: domino, water and light gates have been built, but real ones need care with timing, and with a signal that grows weaker at every step.
halt.r.empty: no blocks: it stops at once
halt.r.press: Run the program to see both.
halt.r.cap: Both lanes count steps on one scale, ten times more at each mark. The agent stops looking at its budget; the program goes on to its end, or forever.
halt.blk.ask: ask the agent about this program, do the opposite
halt.msg2.stops: It stopped within the budget, and the agent saw it: right.
halt.msg2.never: It never stops, and the agent guessed so: right, this time.
halt.msg2.fooled: The agent gave up at {b} steps and guessed "never". The program stopped after {n}: fooled. A bigger budget only moves the wall.
halt.msg2.self: To answer, the agent must run this very program, which first asks the agent again, so its answer never comes within its budget. It guesses "never", and the program, told so, stops. Whatever the budget, whatever the method: fooled.
halt.open.k: What else is in this class
halt.open.p1: No program can tell, for every program, whether it stops. The same holds for any question about what a program does, rather than how it is written (Rice, 1953): whether it ever crashes, leaks a secret, or computes what its maker meant.
halt.open.p2: So no checker can be sure of every design an AI hands it. What can be done: check designs small or regular enough to bound, prove properties of the ones built to be proved, and test the rest. When a system is too complex to inspect, what can trust rest on?
halt.hint.fool: Make the program count to more steps than the agent's budget, and then stop.
halt.hint.more: Give the agent a bigger budget, then count higher than that.
halt.hint.self: Clear the program and use the last block: ask the agent about this very program, and do the opposite.
halt.done: All three fooled. However large the budget, however clever the agent, the program built on it proves it wrong: Turing's argument of 1936.
halt.note2: Turing, On computable numbers (1936, doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230); Rice's theorem (1953). The blocks become RISC-V instructions on the lab's simulator, and the ask is one call the lab answers. This agent only runs and guesses; Turing's proof covers any method at all.
ear.cover: Listen. What is this block doing?
ear.why.busy: A sum on every tick, and the fetches hidden behind the work.
ear.why.wait: A thump, then gaps: the work stops while the data travels.
ear.why.hot: A louder, higher hum, more hiss, and sharp clicks: wrong bits.
ear.why.saving: The ticks come half as fast, and the hum is low and quiet.
ear.nosound: No sound came from this device. Turn the sound on and play again; on a phone, check it is not on silent.
ear.run: Your answers, oldest first: each column is as tall as your share right of the last ten at that answer. The line is the goal.
ear.hidAria: The block, hidden while you listen
ear.picAria: The block, {state}, its parts lit in time with the sound
ear.hint: Listen for three things: gaps between the soft blips (waiting), how fast the ticks come (saving power), and sharp clicks over a higher hum (too hot). Busy has none of them.
rv.introJob: This core runs inside a machine. {job}: its program already works. Run it, then Play to watch each instruction go through the core's datapath; the puzzles beside it are yours to write. Every run is made twice: on the lab's reference core, and on the core made of your own ALU slice.
rv.fig.ref: the arithmetic unit is your slice, 32 copies
rv.fig.right: the arithmetic unit is your slice, 32 copies: every row of it right
rv.fig.wrong: the arithmetic unit is your slice, 32 copies: {n} rows of it wrong
rv.fig.cap: Each instruction is a light: fetched from the program, its registers read, worked out by the 32 slices (a lit slice gave a 1), through memory if it needs it, and written back. A branch that jumps lights the wire back to the program.
rv.f.unread: Your slice does not read as a circuit, so your core cannot be built. Turn its gates back, or start again from the lab's example.
rv.f.same: Your core gave the reference core's answer on every case.
rv.f.quiet: Your core gave the reference core's answer on every case, though {n} rows of your slice are wrong: this program never asked for them. Another program would.
rv.f.where: On the case {c}, at step {k}: line {l}, {op}. Until then the two cores agreed on every register.
rv.f.alu: The arithmetic unit was asked to {op} {p} and {q}: it gave {got} where {want} is right.
rv.f.slice: Slice {n} is where it started: handed a = {a}, b = {b} and a carry in of {c}, it gave the answer bit {y} and the carry out {cy}, where an ALU slice must give {wy} and {wc}. Every slice is the same design, so the same row is wrong in all 32.
rv.s.d: One bit of the arithmetic unit, copied 32 times. Tap a gate to turn it into another kind (AND, OR, XOR), and the programs run again on your core: see which still give the right answer, and where the first wrong one began.
rv.hint.job: Press Run, then Play, and follow the light. Then turn a gate of your slice and run it again: does the machine still get its answer?
rv.dp.jump: back to the program: the branch jumps
rv.job.hearing.d: Two microphones hear the same sound; the core keeps the louder of the two readings (a1, a2) in a0.
rv.job.wildfire.d: Six smoke readings wait in memory from address 4096; the core counts how many are over the alarm level in a2.
rv.job.rover.d: Three computers give an answer (a1, a2, a3); the core keeps, bit by bit, what at least two of them agree on.
rv.job.radio.d: Five signal readings wait in memory from address 4096; the core finds the strongest.
rev.intro: An ordinary gate takes in more bits than it gives out: an AND takes two and gives one, so its output cannot tell what came in. The lost bit is erased, and physics charges at least kT ln 2 of heat for each bit erased (Landauer's limit; k is Boltzmann's constant, T the temperature): about 3 zeptojoules at room temperature. A Toffoli gate erases nothing: it passes its bits through and flips one of them, its target, only when its two controls are both 1. Run it again and it undoes itself.
rev.predict: An ordinary adder erases at least one bit every time it adds, so it can never spend less than that floor. An adder made only of Toffoli gates erases nothing. Run slowly enough, can it spend less than the floor?
rev.guess.0: No: nothing goes under the floor
rev.guess.1: Yes, if each step is slow enough
rev.right: Your guess holds. The floor is the price of erasing, and this adder erases nothing, so physics sets it no floor: the slower each step, the less it loses, with no limit. On the chart below its line passes under an ordinary adder's floor once each step takes about a microsecond. What it pays instead is time.
rev.wrong: Not so: it can, at room temperature. The floor is the price of erasing, and this adder erases nothing, so physics sets it no floor: the slower each step, the less it loses, with no limit. On the chart below its line passes under an ordinary adder's floor once each step takes about a microsecond. What it pays instead is time.
rev.aria: Four wires and the gates on them: {g} gates, adding right on {n} of the 8 inputs.
rev.cell: {w}, place {n}: tap for a control, again for the target, again to clear
rev.legend: Bits flow from left to right; a lit wire carries a 1. On each gate a dot is a control and the ringed plus its target, flipped (and lit warm) when every control is 1. A Toffoli has two controls; with one of them held at 1 it is the simpler CNOT. The spare wire starts at 0. Tap a place on a wire once for a control, twice for the target, three times to clear it.
rev.tap: Every input, what an adder must give, and what your circuit gives. Tap a row to watch it flow along the wires.
rev.msg.bad: A gate has one target and at most two controls: the red one does nothing until it is mended.
rev.msg.half: This is a half adder: it adds a and b, and leaves the carry in out. Two more gates will bring it in.
rev.msg.rows: Right on {n} of 8 inputs. Watch a wrong row flow along the wires, and ask which wire should have flipped.
rev.msg.fast: It adds, and erases nothing; but each step switches so fast that it loses only {v} times less than switching at once. Slow the steps down.
rev.msg.slow: It loses {v} times less, but a faster step would still save 100 times, and every step slower costs time. Find the fastest that still does it.
rev.msg.met: It adds, erases nothing, and loses {v} times less than switching at once, at the fastest steps that do it. The price is time: one addition takes {time}.
rev.set.ramp: Time for each step: how slowly a wire is charged
rev.chart.aria: The energy of one addition against the time of each step: now {e}; the floor of an ordinary adder is {f}.
rev.chart.floor: floor of an adder that erases
rev.chart.legend: The energy one addition loses against how slowly each step charges its wire, on scales where each grid line is a thousand times the last. Switched at once (grey), a wire loses half the energy it is charged with, however long you wait; ramped slowly (blue), it loses less the slower it goes. The red line is the least an ordinary adder can spend, kT ln 2 for the bit it erases; under it (shaded) only logic that erases nothing can go. A femtojoule (fJ) is a thousand attojoules (aJ), and an attojoule a thousand zeptojoules (zJ); a nanosecond (ns) is a thousand picoseconds (ps).
rev.sum: One addition now loses {e}: {x} times less than switching at once, and {f}.
rev.sum.over: {v} times the floor of an adder that erases
rev.sum.under: {v} times under the floor of an adder that erases
rev.time: {g} gates, one step each: one addition takes {time}, as long as {ticks} ticks of a {ghz} GHz clock.
rev.hint: The spare wire already holds a AND b, and wire b holds a XOR b. Add a Toffoli with its controls on b and on the carry in and its target on the spare wire: that wire becomes the carry out. Then a CNOT from b onto the carry in turns it into the sum. Then slow the steps until it loses 100 times less, and no slower.
rev.done: The adder erases nothing: run backwards, it gives a, b and the carry in back. Ramped slowly it loses a hundred times less than switching at once, and slower still it passes under the floor an ordinary adder can never cross. That is the promise of reversible computing, and its price: every step takes time, and a larger circuit needs more wires to keep what it would otherwise have erased.
rev.note: A teaching model. Each gate is one step that charges one wire of 1 femtofarad through 1 kilohm to 0.7 volts: switched at once it loses half the energy it is charged with, ramped over a time T it loses about RC/T of the energy on it (adiabatic charging; RC, the wire's own time, is 1 ps). Left out: the circuit that makes the slow ramps, which must recover energy too; leaks, which grow with time and limit how far slower helps; and the extra wires a larger reversible circuit keeps. A reversible test chip has recovered part of its energy this way.
dfl.intro: A model like those behind chat assistants is mostly numbers called weights, and every answer reads all of them. A processor keeps them in memory off the chip and fetches each one again for every answer, and fetching a number costs far more energy than computing with it. A dataflow chip lays the model's layers across its tiles instead: each tile is a small processor with memory of its own, holds part of one layer, and passes its results on to the tile holding the next, so the weights never move.
dfl.predict: A chip holds nine of a model's ten layers. The tenth is fetched from memory off the chip every time the model answers. How much of the energy of an answer goes on that one layer?
dfl.right: Your guess holds: {p} of it. Fetching a bit from memory off the chip costs about {x} times reading it from a tile's own memory, so the one layer left out outweighs the nine kept in.
dfl.wrong: Most of it: {p}. Fetching a bit from memory off the chip costs about {x} times reading it from a tile's own memory, so the one layer left out outweighs the nine kept in.
dfl.aria: A chip of {n} tiles holding a model of {l} layers: {p} of its weights on the chip.
dfl.legend: Each square is a tile with 2 MB of memory; a layer of the model, 4 MB of weights, fills two, numbered in the order the numbers flow through them, and the line is their way from layer to layer. What does not fit waits in memory off the chip (right) and is fetched again for every answer. An MB, a megabyte, holds a million weights here.
dfl.msg.spill: {p} of the weights fit; the rest is fetched from memory for every answer, and takes {s} of its energy.
dfl.msg.room: The whole model fits, with {free} tiles to spare. How large a model does this chip hold?
dfl.msg.try: The whole model fits, and fills the chip. Is it the largest? Try one layer more.
dfl.msg.met: The largest model this chip holds whole: {l} layers, {mb} MB. One layer more, and its weights come from memory at {x} times the energy for every answer.
dfl.e.on: read from a tile's own memory
dfl.e.share: {p} of this goes on the {mb} MB fetched from off the chip. A µJ is a microjoule, a millionth of a joule.
dfl.e.none: Every weight is read where it is kept: {x} times less than fetching each one. A µJ is a microjoule, a millionth of a joule.
dfl.hint: Make the model larger one layer at a time and watch the chip fill. When a layer has nowhere to go, step back one: that is the largest model this chip holds.
dfl.done: Kept on the chip, a model costs a fraction of fetching it; one layer too many, and fetching takes most of the energy again. That is why chips built this way carry as much memory as they can, some a whole wafer of it, and why a model that outgrows them loses the gain: the models people train grow faster than the memory on any one chip.
dfl.note: A model with energies for a 45 nm chip from a published table: reading 16 bits from a large memory on the chip, and from memory off it. Only the weights are counted, each read once per answer. Left out: the arithmetic, the numbers passed from tile to tile, the memory a processor keeps close to its cores, and the many answers it can serve from one fetch (batching), all of which narrow the gap. Real chips built this way hold from hundreds of megabytes to tens of gigabytes.
para.job.exact.d: Spreadsheets, browsers, operating systems: millions of different instructions, every bit must be right.
para.fit.exact.cpu: Built for exactly this: any program, exact answers.
para.fit.exact.gpu: Only the parallel parts speed up.
para.fit.exact.spatial: Shines on regular data flows, not branchy code.
para.fit.exact.reversible: Could in principle run anything with far less energy, but only test chips exist.
para.job.llm.d: Hundreds of billions of weights, read again for every token, to millions of users.
para.fit.llm.gpu: Today's workhorse: huge memory bandwidth and mature software.
para.fit.llm.spatial: Wafer-scale and SRAM dataflow chips keep weights on chip and lead on speed per user.
para.fit.llm.cim: Great for small models; big models outgrow the arrays and need exact digital steps too.
para.fit.llm.photonic: Fast, low-power matrix math, but converting to and from light costs energy and precision.
para.fit.llm.reversible: A long-term route to lower energy per operation.
para.job.sense: Listen for a wake word for a year on a coin cell
para.job.sense.d: Always on, almost always silence, a tiny battery.
para.fit.sense.neuro: Spikes only when sound changes: microwatts while idle.
para.fit.sense.cim: Small analog arrays run tiny networks very efficiently.
para.fit.sense.cpu: A low-power microcontroller with a small network works today.
para.fit.sense.reversible: Would cut energy further one day.
para.job.sample.d: Find a good schedule or route among billions, or draw samples for a generative model.
para.fit.sample.pbits: Noise is the engine: p-bits explore many answers in parallel and settle into good ones.
para.fit.sample.gpu: Runs sampling algorithms well, at a high energy cost.
para.fit.sample.quantum: Annealers and some algorithms may help; a clear advantage is still debated.
para.fit.sample.cpu: Classic heuristics work, slowly for big problems.
para.fit.sample.cim: Analog noise can be put to use.
para.fit.sample.photonic: Optical Ising machines are a research topic.
para.job.chem.d: Electrons behave quantum-mechanically; the cost of exact simulation explodes with size.
para.fit.chem.quantum: The original reason to build quantum computers. Needs error-corrected machines, planned for around 2029.
para.fit.chem.gpu: Approximate methods and AI models work well for many molecules.
para.fit.chem.cpu: Classic simulation codes, limited by exponential cost.
para.job.learn: Learn from a few examples on almost no energy
para.job.learn.d: What brains do: adapt continuously, from little data, on about 20 watts.
para.fit.learn.bio: Real neurons learn by themselves; controlling and scaling them is the open problem.
para.fit.learn.neuro: On-chip learning rules are a core research goal.
para.fit.learn.gpu: Can learn anything, with lots of data and energy.
para.fit.learn.cim: Analog weights can be updated in place, with drift and noise to manage.
para.gallery.super.d: Currents flow with zero resistance in metals cooled to a few kelvin; logic switches with single flux quanta.
para.gallery.super.signal: An imec-led team targets about 100× better energy efficiency for AI data centers, even after paying for cooling.
para.gallery.super.catch: Everything must be cooled to near absolute zero, and the circuits are far less dense than CMOS.
para.gallery.bio.d: Human neurons grown on an electrode array learn from electrical feedback.
para.gallery.bio.signal: Cortical Labs released the CL1 in March 2025, a biological computer sold for about $35,000.
para.gallery.bio.catch: Cells live for months, behave differently each time, and raise ethical questions.
para.gallery.dna.d: Data is written as sequences of the four DNA bases: an exabyte could fit in a few grams.
para.gallery.dna.signal: Biomemory plans its first commercial DNA storage in data centers in the second half of 2026.
para.gallery.dna.catch: Writing and reading take hours and cost far more than tape today.
para.gallery.spin.d: Uses the magnetic spin of electrons instead of charge, so states survive without power.
para.gallery.spin.signal: Magnetic memory (MRAM) already ships inside microcontrollers; spin logic is still in labs.
para.gallery.spin.catch: Switching is slower and less reliable than transistors.
para.gallery.memristor.d: Resistors that remember: a grid of them stores weights and multiplies in one step.
para.gallery.memristor.signal: The core of many compute-in-memory prototypes.
para.gallery.memristor.catch: Values drift over time and differ from device to device.
para.gallery.stoch.d: Numbers become random bit streams; a single AND gate multiplies two of them.
para.gallery.stoch.signal: Used in research for tiny, fault-tolerant circuits.
para.gallery.stoch.catch: Precision needs long streams, which costs time.
para.gallery.reservoir.d: Let a physical system, such as a laser, a spin wave or a bucket of water, transform the input, and train only a simple readout.
para.gallery.reservoir.signal: Many lab demos on time-series prediction.
para.gallery.reservoir.catch: Hard to make reliable, programmable and large.
para.gallery.analog.d: Voltages stand for numbers; circuits solve equations continuously instead of step by step.
para.gallery.analog.signal: Small companies sell analog computers again for differential equations and control.
para.gallery.analog.catch: Noise limits precision, and each problem needs rewiring.
para.gallery.anneal.d: Thousands of qubits relax into low-energy states that encode optimization answers.
para.gallery.anneal.catch: Whether they beat good classical methods is still debated.
para.gallery.approx.d: Accept small errors where nobody notices them, and save energy and area.
para.gallery.approx.signal: Already mainstream in AI: 8-, 4- and even fewer-bit numbers.
para.gallery.approx.catch: Only works where errors are tolerable.
para.gallery.optnn.d: Light passes through printed layers that diffract it into an answer: computing at the speed of light, with no power for the math.
para.gallery.optnn.catch: Fixed once printed; hard to train and scale.
para.gallery.molecular.d: Molecules or chemical reactions carry out logic.
para.gallery.molecular.signal: Research curiosity since DNA computing in 1994.
para.gallery.molecular.catch: Very slow, and hard to read out.

ckp.power.runs: Runs, up to {f} GHz at {v} V
ckp.stall.load: {ins} needs x{reg} from {from}: {cycles} stall cycle(s). A load's data only exists after the memory stage, so even forwarding must wait one cycle.
ckp.stall.nofwd: {ins} needs x{reg} from {from}: {cycles} stall cycle(s). Without forwarding it must wait for write-back.
ckp.stall.none: No stalls. Every instruction gets its inputs just in time.
ckp.hint.latch.oscillate: Both released at the same instant: each gate keeps flipping the other, forever in this model. A real latch settles after a while, at random. That is why designs never set and reset at once.
ckp.hint.latch.both: Both on: Q and not-Q are both 0, which a latch should never be. Now turn both off at once.
ckp.hint.latch.setting: S is on, so Q becomes 1. Now turn S off and see whether Q stays.
ckp.hint.latch.resetting: R is on, so Q becomes 0. Turn R off: does it stay 0?
ckp.hint.latch.unknown: At power-on Q is unknown: nothing has set it yet. Turn S on.
ckp.hint.latch.memory: Both off, and Q holds whatever was written last. Two gates, one bit of memory: a processor's registers are built from loops like this.
ckp.hint.latch.holds1: S is off, but Q is still 1: the loop keeps it alive. That is one bit of memory. Now try R.
ckp.hint.latch.holds0: Q is 0 and stays 0. Turn S on to store a 1.
ckp.hint.flop.none: Switch D to 1 in one slot. The dashed lines are the ticks.
ckp.hint.flop.one-done: D was steady for 600 ps before the tick, longer than the setup time, so the first latch had settled when the clock rose.
ckp.hint.flop.late: D rose exactly at the tick: too late. The first latch closes as the clock rises, so D must be there a little before.
ckp.hint.flop.before: The flip-flop looks at D only as the clock rises. Put the 1 in the slot just before a tick.
ckp.hint.flop.differ-done: The latch let a late change through while the clock was 1; the flip-flop had already taken its value at the tick.
ckp.hint.flop.differ: Hint: the latch is open the whole time the clock is 1. What if D changes in the second half of the last cycle?
ckp.hint.flop.free: Count the changes: the latch passes every wiggle while the clock is 1; the flip-flop changes at most once per tick.
ckp.goal.one.why: Make the flip-flop store a 1 with D at 1 for only one slot.
ckp.goal.free.why: Draw any pattern on D and compare the latch with the flip-flop.
ckp.ch.slowCorner.goal: At a 4 GHz clock, add the fewest pipeline registers that still pass sign-off on a hot, low-voltage chip. What does it cost in latency?
ckp.ch.slowCorner.done: Two registers pass at the slow corner, at the cost of 3 cycles of latency instead of 2. Sign-off must pass at the slow corner, because some chips will run hot at low voltage.
ckp.ch.zeroStalls.goal: Get the program through the 5-stage pipeline with no stall cycles at all. Which two fixes does it take?
ckp.ch.zeroStalls.done: It takes both forwarding and reordering. Forwarding hands a result on before it is written back; reordering moves an independent instruction into the gap a load leaves.
ckp.ch.latch.goal: Store a 1 in two NOR gates, let go, and watch it stay. Then set and reset at once.
ckp.ch.latch.done: Two gates held a bit; set and reset together, they oscillate. Designs never do that.
ckp.ch.oneSlot.goal: Make a flip-flop store a 1 with its input at 1 for only one time slot.
ckp.ch.oneSlot.done: The flip-flop took the 1 at the tick, because D was steady for longer than the setup time.
ckp.ch.differ.goal: Make the latch and the flip-flop end with different values.
ckp.ch.differ.done: The latch let a late change through while the clock was 1; the flip-flop had already taken its value.

ar.opt.shape.swarm.d: many small parts loosely joined, so one can fail

br.intro: One spec, two matters. The same truth table runs in silicon, as the bench's gates, and in a test tube of DNA strands. In the tube, an input strand pushes an output strand off its partner (strand displacement); a threshold strand soaks up the first part of the input, so only a clear signal passes; fuel strands free the input again, so even a weak one releases a full output; and fuel slowly frees outputs with no input at all (a leak). A reporter turns the output into light: above the top line it reads 1, below the bottom one 0, and between them it cannot tell.
br.spec.choice: The choice: a if s, else b
br.aria: Silicon and the test tube side by side: {n} of {of} inputs right in the tube
br.legend: Left: the gates in silicon, lit by the chosen input. Right: the tube's output for every input over two hours, each at its worst amounts, the chosen one bold and red where it reads wrong. The band between the lines is too dim to call.
br.msg.met: Both answer right in the tube, on every input, in time: one spec, two matters.
br.msg.leak: A row that should be 0 lights up: the threshold lets one input through, or the fuel leaks. Raise the threshold, or give less fuel.
br.msg.blur: Some answers are too dim to call. A 0 that glows is a leak (less fuel, or a higher threshold); a 1 that stays dim needs more fuel or a lower threshold.
br.msg.weak: A row that should be 1 never gets bright: too little passes the threshold, or nothing frees the input again. Lower the threshold, or give the gate fuel.
br.msg.slow: Right on every input, but the slowest 1 takes longer than {v} minutes. Fuel speeds a gate up.
br.msg.other: This one is right, and in time. Now {spec}.
br.cmp.si: {ps} ps, exact on every input, {n} transistors, made in a factory.
br.cmp.tube: {m} to answer, read as light. Strands are made without a factory and can work in a drop of liquid, even a sample from a living thing, where a chip cannot go.
br.cmp.tubeNo: No answer yet: an input that should give 1 never gets over its line.
br.slower: For the choice, the tube is about {x} times slower than silicon.
br.src.seesaw: Qian and Winfree built logic this way in 2011, every gate with a threshold and fuel, up to a circuit of 130 strands that takes the square root of a four-bit number.
br.src.cello: In living cells, the tool Cello compiles a circuit written in Verilog, the language chips are written in, into DNA for E. coli bacteria: of 60 circuits it designed, 45 worked on every input (2016).
br.hint: An AND gets 2 units when both inputs are 1 and 1 unit when only one is: a threshold between them (about 1.2) holds back the single input. Give the AND some fuel to lift its output, but not so much that it leaks. The OR adds what the two ANDs give, so its threshold must sit above what they leak (about 0.4 to 0.7), with fuel of its own.
br.done: The same choice runs in both matters. Silicon answers in a third of a nanosecond, exact every time; the tube takes most of an hour and needs every gate tuned, but its gates are molecules, made without a factory.
br.note: A model with honest trends, not a chemistry simulator. Amounts are in units of one input; each strand is pipetted within a tenth of its amount, so every input is tried at its worst; the rates and leaks are the lab's own choices. The tube has no NOT, so the choice gets s as two strands, one for 1 and one for 0. Silicon is the bench's own cell library, at 130 nm.
bw.intro: A tube that recognizes shapes, by winner takes all. Each memory is a set of weight strands, one for each pixel of the shape it remembers, so a pattern's pixel strands make each memory's sum. An annihilator strand removes one unit of two sums together: the smaller sum is wiped out and only the largest is left. A restoring gate, a threshold and fuel as in the logic, lights the winner.

bw.src: Cherry and Qian sorted 10 × 10 pictures of handwritten digits into up to nine kinds this way, with up to 30 of the 100 bits flipped (2018).
bw.hint: With no annihilator, two memories light for shapes that look alike. Give about one unit of annihilator or more, so each smaller sum is wiped out; keep the threshold low, since the winner is left with only its lead; and keep the fuel near half a unit, so the winner gets bright and the others do not leak.
bw.done: Every shape lit only its own memory. No threshold alone could do it: a loser in one shape summed as much as a winner in another. The annihilators weighed the sums against each other, as a winner-take-all network does.
